items.title: The Pushyabhuti (Vardhana) Dynasty & Thanesar
items.body:
## Origins at Thanesar

- Harshavardhan (**Harsha**) was born in **590 CE at Thanesar** (Sthanvishvara), in present-day **Haryana**.
- He belonged to the **Pushyabhuti dynasty**, also called the **Vardhana dynasty**, which ruled a **small kingdom in northern India**.
- His father **Prabhakarvardhan** was the ruler of Thanesar, and his elder brother **Rajyavardhan** was the crown prince.
- The dynasty's early seat was **Thanesar**; Harsha would later shift the political centre to **Kannauj**.

figure.alt: Map of the Empire of Harshavardhana alongside an illustrated portrait of the king
figure.caption: The Pushyabhuti (Vardhana) ruler Harshavardhana and the extent of his empire, seated originally at Thanesar (Sthanvishvara).

keyPoints: Harsha born 590 CE at Thanesar (Sthanvishvara), present-day Haryana.
Belonged to the Pushyabhuti dynasty, also called the Vardhana dynasty.
Father Prabhakarvardhan ruled Thanesar; elder brother Rajyavardhan was crown prince.
Dynasty's original seat was Thanesar; capital later shifted to Kannauj.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Reign of Harshavardhana (Early Life and Ascension)

items.title: Harsha's Rise (606 CE) & the Harsha Era
items.body:
## Ascension at Sixteen

- After the **death of his brother Rajyavardhan** and the **assassination of his sister's husband Grahavarman**, Harsha ascended the throne of Thanesar at the young age of **16** — **c. 606 CE**.
- Initially his rule was confined to the **small kingdom of Thanesar**, but he harboured ambitions of **uniting northern India**.
- His accession in **606 CE** is traditionally taken as the beginning of the **Harsha era** (Harshabda), a reckoning of years used in later records.
- He grew into a **capable conqueror and administrator**, eventually forging one of the last great empires of northern India.
keyPoints: Ascended the Thanesar throne at age 16, c. 606 CE.
Rise followed the death of brother Rajyavardhan and murder of Grahavarman.
606 CE marks the start of the Harsha era (Harshabda).
Began confined to Thanesar but aimed to unite northern India.
items.mnemonic: '606 = Sixteen & Sovereign' — Harsha crowned, Harsha era begins.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Reign of Harshavardhana (Early Life and Ascension)

items.title: Political Expansion — From Thanesar to Kannauj
items.body:
## Uniting Northern India

- Harsha's **first campaign was against Shashanka of Gauda**, to avenge his brother Rajyavardhan's killing and his sister **Rajyashri's** kidnapping; he allied with **Bhaskaravarman, the Kamarupa king**, and Shashanka was defeated.
- He then **claimed the sovereignty of Kannauj**, **united Thanesar and Kannauj**, and made **Kannauj his capital**.
- He brought many independent kingdoms under his command — controlling **Punjab and central India**, and **annexing Bengal, Bihar and Odisha**.
- He also **defeated the Vallabhi king in Gujarat**, extending his influence westward.

figure.alt: Detailed map of Harshavardhana's empire 606 CE to 647 CE with capital Kannauj, Sthanvishvara, Magadha and the Narmada boundary
figure.caption: Harshavardhana's empire (606–647 CE): capital at Kannauj, spanning the Ganges plains up to the Narmada in the south.

keyPoints: First campaign against Shashanka of Gauda; allied with Bhaskaravarman of Kamarupa.
United Thanesar and Kannauj; made Kannauj his capital.
Controlled Punjab and central India; annexed Bengal, Bihar and Odisha.
Defeated the Vallabhi king in Gujarat.
items.mnemonic: Shashanka first, then Kannauj capital — 'Bengal-Bihar-Odisha + Vallabhi'.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Reign of Harshavardhana (Political expansion)

items.title: Defeat by Pulakeshin II & the Narmada Boundary
items.body:
## The Southern Check

- Harsha's northern conquests were unbroken, but he **failed to conquer the south**.
- The **Chalukya king Pulakeshin II** defeated Harsha in **618–619 CE**, halting his southward advance.
- This defeat **restricted Harsha's southern territorial extent up to the Narmada River**, which became the effective boundary between the two powers.
- Pulakeshin II ruled from the Chalukya capital **Vatapi**; the clash is a landmark of north–south political balance in the 7th century.
keyPoints: Harsha failed to expand into the south of India.
Chalukya king Pulakeshin II defeated Harsha in 618–619 CE.
The defeat fixed Harsha's southern limit at the Narmada River.
Pulakeshin II's Chalukya capital was Vatapi.
items.mnemonic: 'Pulakeshin pushed Harsha back to the Narmada' — south stayed Chalukya.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Reign of Harshavardhana (Political expansion; Contemporary Kingdoms)

items.title: Banabhatta — Harshacharita & Kadambari
items.body:
## The Court Poet

- **Banabhatta (c. 606–647 CE)** was a **poet in Harsha's court** and one of the great Sanskrit prose writers.
- His principal work **Harshacharita** ('Deeds of Harsha') is a **biography of Harsha**, giving an account of his life and deeds **in the form of verses**.
- He also wrote **Kadambari**, regarded as **one of the world's earliest novels**.
- Harsha's patronage of art and literature attracted many artists, of whom Banabhatta is the most celebrated.
keyPoints: Banabhatta (c. 606–647 CE) was a poet in Harsha's court.
Harshacharita = biography of Harsha ('Deeds of Harsha'), written in verse.
Kadambari = one of the world's earliest novels.
Harsha's patronage of art and literature drew many artists to his court.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Reign of Harshavardhana (Literature — Banabhatta)

items.title: Hiuen-Tsang (Xuanzang) & the Si-Yu-Ki
items.body:
## The Prince of Pilgrims

- **Hiuen-Tsang (Xuanzang)** was a **Chinese pilgrim** who spent nearly **13 years in India (630–643 CE)** during Harsha's reign.
- He collected **sacred texts and relics** to take back to China and was called the **"prince of pilgrims"** for visiting sites associated with the life of the Buddha.
- His work **Si-Yu-Ki** gives detailed information on the **social, economic, religious and cultural** conditions of Harsha's India.
- His observations: **Nalanda** was the leading university; **Prayag and Kanauj** rose as important centres while **Pataliputra and Vaishali** declined; he even records that **he was robbed once**, noting law and order were imperfect.
keyPoints: Hiuen-Tsang (Xuanzang) was a Chinese pilgrim in India c. 630–643 CE (~13 years).
Wrote the Si-Yu-Ki, a key source on Harsha's social/economic/religious life.
Called the 'prince of pilgrims'; came to visit Buddhist sites.
Noted Nalanda as the leading university; Prayag & Kanauj rising, Pataliputra & Vaishali declining.
items.mnemonic: Xuanzang = 'Prince of Pilgrims', 13 years (630–643), wrote Si-Yu-Ki.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Reign of Harshavardhana (Hiuen Tsang's Si-Yu-Ki)

items.title: Patronage of Nalanda & Education
items.body:
## Learning in the Monasteries

- **Nalanda** was, in Hiuen-Tsang's account, the **notable leading educational university** of Harsha's time, and Harsha was a major patron of it.
- **Education was imparted in the monasteries** and was largely **religious** in character; much religious literature was produced.
- The **Vedas were taught orally** and not written down; **Sanskrit** was the language of the learned.
- A student's learning typically ran **between the ages of 9 and 30**, and many devoted their whole lives to study; wandering **bhikkhus and sadhus** were respected for their wisdom.
keyPoints: Nalanda was the leading educational university, patronised by Harsha.
Education was monastery-based and largely religious.
Vedas taught orally; Sanskrit was the language of the learned.
Learning spanned ages 9–30; the I-Tsing biographies describe Nalanda's monks.
items.mnemonic: 'Nalanda = No.1 university' — Harsha's great educational patronage.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Reign of Harshavardhana (Education; Hiuen Tsang's observations; I-Tsing)

items.title: The Kannauj & Prayag Assemblies
items.body:
## Great Religious Gatherings

- Under Harsha, **Prayag and Kanauj** became the **important religious and cultural centres** of the empire (as Pataliputra and Vaishali declined).
- Harsha convened a grand **assembly at Kannauj**, held in honour of **Hiuen-Tsang** and to promote **Mahayana Buddhism**, attended by kings, monks and scholars.
- He is renowned for the **assembly at Prayag** (the Prayag/Allahabad convocation), a great **quinquennial distribution of charity** where the king gave away the royal treasury as alms.
- These assemblies reflect Harsha's **secular patronage** — he respected all faiths even after embracing Buddhism.
keyPoints: Prayag and Kanauj were the key religious/cultural centres under Harsha.
The Kannauj assembly honoured Hiuen-Tsang and promoted Mahayana Buddhism.
The Prayag assembly was a great charitable convocation of alms-giving.
The assemblies show Harsha's secular, all-faith patronage.
items.mnemonic: Two assemblies — 'Kannauj for the pilgrim, Prayag for charity'.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Reign of Harshavardhana (Hiuen Tsang's observations — Prayag & Kanauj as centres; religion)

items.title: Harsha the Author — Nagananda, Ratnavali & Priyadarshika
items.body:
## Three Sanskrit Plays

- Harsha was himself a **great scholar and noted author** who wrote **three Sanskrit plays**: **Ratnavali**, **Priyadarshika** and **Nagananda**.
- **Ratnavali** ('Precious Garland') is a drama about a beautiful princess **Ratnavali** and King **Udayana**; it is divided into **four acts** and contains early references to the **festival of colours (Holi)**.
- **Priyadarshika** and **Nagananda** complete his dramatic corpus; Nagananda is noted for its **Buddhist theme** (self-sacrifice of the prince Jimutavahana).
- His authorship reflects the **literary efflorescence** of his court, alongside poets like Banabhatta.
keyPoints: Harsha wrote three Sanskrit plays: Ratnavali, Priyadarshika and Nagananda.
Ratnavali ('Precious Garland') — princess Ratnavali and King Udayana, in four acts.
Ratnavali contains an early reference to Holi, the festival of colours.
Nagananda carries a Buddhist theme; Harsha was both patron and author.
items.mnemonic: 'N-R-P' — Nagananda, Ratnavali, Priyadarshika: Harsha's three plays.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Reign of Harshavardhana (author of 3 Sanskrit plays; Ratnavali)

items.title: Administration, Revenue & Feudalism
items.body:
## A Decentralised, Feudalising Polity

- Harsha kept **strong central authority** but the polity was increasingly **feudalised and decentralised**; the empire was divided into provinces (**Bhuktis**) under **Governors**, districts (**Vishayas**) under **Vishayapatis**, and villages under headmen (**Gramikas**).
- He was assisted by a **Mantri Parishad (Council of Ministers)**; key officials included **Avanti** (foreign relations & war), **Simhanada** (commander-in-chief) and **Skandagupta** (chief of the elephant force).
- **Three main taxes** were levied: **Bhaga** (land tax, one-sixth of produce), **Hiranya** (cash tax from farmers/merchants) and **Bali** (an additional/oppressive tax).
- Large land grants (**Agraharas**) to Brahmins and Buddhists spread **feudalism**, which is why **few coins** were issued by Harsha; his army had ~**100,000 cavalry, 50,000 infantry and 60,000 elephants**.
keyPoints: Provinces = Bhuktis (Governors); districts = Vishayas (Vishayapatis); villages under Gramikas.
Assisted by a Mantri Parishad; Avanti (war/foreign), Simhanada (C-in-C), Skandagupta (elephants).
Three taxes: Bhaga (land, 1/6 produce), Hiranya (cash), Bali (additional).
Land grants (Agraharas) spread feudalism; few coins issued; huge army of cavalry, infantry & elephants.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Reign of Harshavardhana (Administration; Economy; Military; Feudalism)

items.title: Decline & Legacy of Harsha's Empire
items.body:
## The Last Great North Indian Empire

- Harsha's empire **began to decline after his death in 647 CE**; since he had **no heirs**, it **disintegrated into smaller regional kingdoms**.
- He is remembered as **one of the last great rulers of northern India** before the Islamic invasions.
- His reign was marked by **peace, prosperity and cultural achievement** that left a lasting impact on Indian history.
- His **patronage of the arts and of Nalanda University** cemented his place as a key figure in India's intellectual history.
keyPoints: Empire declined after Harsha's death in 647 CE; he left no heirs.
It disintegrated into smaller regional kingdoms (feudatories).
Remembered as one of the last great rulers of northern India before Islamic invasions.
Legacy: patronage of arts and Nalanda University; an age of peace and prosperity.
items.mnemonic: '647 & no heir' — empire splinters; Harsha = last great northern emperor.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Reign of Harshavardhana (Decline and Legacy)
